XIV.1.title: What is shameful
XIV.1.reflection: Yuan Xian, the disciple Legge calls Hsien, asks what is shameful. To draw a salary when the state has the Way, and to draw one when it has lost the Way. Taking pay from a bad government, or taking it from a good one without contributing, are both shameful.
XIV.1.question: When would taking your pay be shameful?

XIV.2.title: Difficult, but is it ren?
XIV.2.reflection: Yuan Xian asks whether someone who never gives way to the urge to win, to boast, to resent or to covet could be called ren. That is difficult, says the Master; whether it is ren, I do not know. Restraining bad impulses is not yet the positive good.
XIV.2.question: Which of the four urges have you restrained this week, and what did you do instead?

XIV.3.title: Attached to comfort
XIV.3.reflection: A shi who cherishes his comfort is not worth calling a shi. The scholar's calling is not compatible with putting ease first.
XIV.3.question: What comfort do you protect at the expense of your calling?

XIV.4.title: Speech in bad times
XIV.4.reflection: When the state has the Way, speak boldly and act boldly; when it lacks the Way, act boldly but speak with caution. Integrity in conduct does not change; candour in words is adjusted to danger.
XIV.4.question: When have you had to be careful with words while keeping your conduct unchanged?

XIV.5.title: Virtue and fine words
XIV.5.reflection: The virtuous are sure to speak well, but those who speak well are not necessarily virtuous. The humane are sure to be brave, but the brave are not necessarily humane. The good quality implies the lesser one, not the other way round.
XIV.5.question: Whose fine words have you mistaken for virtue?

XIV.6.title: The archer and the farmers
XIV.6.reflection: Nangong Kuo observes that Yi the archer and Ao the strongman both died violent deaths, while Yu and Ji, who worked the land, came to rule the world. Confucius says nothing, but when Kuo leaves he praises him as a junzi who values virtue. Force ends badly; work and goodness endure.
XIV.6.question: What has endured in your life, force or patient work?

XIV.7.title: Never a small man who is ren
XIV.7.reflection: There have been junzi who were not ren, alas, but never a small man who was. The junzi is not guaranteed goodness; the small man is excluded from it.
XIV.7.question: In what way could you be a good person and still fall short of ren?

XIV.8.title: Love that demands
XIV.8.reflection: Can you love someone without making demands of them? Can you be loyal to someone without instructing them? Love and loyalty both include asking more of the one loved.
XIV.8.question: Whom do you love enough to ask more of them?

XIV.9.title: Four hands on one document
XIV.9.reflection: In Zheng, a state document was drafted by Pi Chen, examined by Shi Shu, polished by Ziyu and finished by Zichan. Four officials, four stages, one text. Good government is careful work done together.
XIV.9.question: Who checks your work before it goes out?

XIV.10.title: Three ministers
XIV.10.reflection: Zichan: a kind man. Zixi: that man, that man, an expression of dismissal. Guan Zhong: he took three hundred households from the Bo family, and their head, living on coarse food, never complained to the end of his life. Even those Guan Zhong took from accepted his judgement as just.
XIV.10.question: Whose judgement against you could you accept without complaint?

XIV.11.title: Poverty without resentment
XIV.11.reflection: To be poor without resentment is hard; to be rich without arrogance is easy. The harder virtue belongs to the one with less.
XIV.11.question: What lack do you carry with some resentment?

XIV.12.title: Fit for one post, not another
XIV.12.reflection: Meng Gongchuo would make an excellent steward in the great families of Zhao or Wei, but not a minister in the small states of Teng or Xue. A good man in one role may be wrong for a smaller and harder one.
XIV.12.question: What role suits you, and which would not?

XIV.13.title: The complete man
XIV.13.reflection: Zilu asks about the complete person. Combine the knowledge of one, the freedom from desire of another, the courage of a third, the skill of a fourth, and refine them with ritual and music. Then the Master lowers the bar: nowadays, one who thinks of rightness when he sees profit, offers his life in danger and keeps an old promise is complete enough.
XIV.13.question: Which of the three present-day marks do you meet?

XIV.14.title: Speaks, laughs, takes, in time
XIV.14.reflection: Is it true that Gongshu Wenzi does not speak, laugh or take? Exaggeration, says his servant: he speaks when it is time, so people do not tire of his speaking; he laughs when there is joy; he takes when it is right. So it is, says Confucius; but is it really so? A doubt remains.
XIV.14.question: Do you speak, laugh and take at the right time?

XIV.15.title: Bargaining with a city
XIV.15.reflection: Zang Wuzhong, holding the fortified town of Fang, asked the duke to name his heir as successor. People say he did not coerce his ruler; I do not believe it. Asking while holding a fortress is a threat in polite form.
XIV.15.question: When has a request of yours been a demand in disguise?

XIV.16.title: Crafty or upright
XIV.16.reflection: Duke Wen of Jin was crafty and not upright; Duke Huan of Qi was upright and not crafty. Two great hegemons, judged by one quality.
XIV.16.question: Would you rather work for a crafty leader or an upright one, and why?

XIV.17.title: Guan Zhong did not die
XIV.17.reflection: Zilu objects: when Duke Huan killed his brother, the minister Shao Hu died with him, but Guan Zhong did not; is he not lacking in ren? Duke Huan gathered the lords together without war chariots, thanks to Guan Zhong: such was his ren, such was his ren. Achievement for the many outweighs a gesture of loyalty.
XIV.17.question: When has doing good for many mattered more than a gesture of loyalty?

XIV.18.title: Buttoning on the left
XIV.18.reflection: Zigong makes the same objection, adding that Guan Zhong even served the man who killed his lord. Confucius: he made his lord leader of the states and set the world in order; the people still enjoy his gifts. Without him we would wear our hair loose and button our robes on the left, like barbarians. Would you hold him to the small faith of ordinary people who kill themselves in a ditch, unknown?
XIV.18.question: Whose larger good have you judged by a smaller rule?

XIV.19.title: Raised beside his master
XIV.19.reflection: Gongshu Wenzi recommended his own steward, Zhuan, so that he rose to be a minister beside him. Hearing it, Confucius says Wenzi deserved the posthumous name Wen, "cultured". Raising a subordinate to one's own level is a mark of culture.
XIV.19.question: Whom could you help rise to stand beside you?

XIV.20.title: Why Duke Ling keeps his state
XIV.20.reflection: Confucius speaks of Duke Ling of Wei's lack of the Way, and Ji Kangzi asks why he does not lose his state. He has Zhongshu Yu for guests, Tuo for the temple, Wangsun Jia for the army: with such men, how could he lose it? Good officials can hold up a bad ruler.
XIV.20.question: Who holds up an institution you know, despite its head?

XIV.21.title: Unashamed words
XIV.21.reflection: Someone who speaks without shame will find it hard to make good on their words. Big talk is a sign of small follow-through.
XIV.21.question: What have you said boldly that is now hard to make good?

XIV.22.title: Reporting a murder
XIV.22.reflection: When Chen Cheng killed the ruler of Qi, Confucius, long retired, bathed and went to court to ask Duke Ai to punish him. The duke sent him to the three families, who refused. Twice Confucius says: since I follow behind the officials, I did not dare not to report it. He does his duty knowing it will fail.
XIV.22.question: What duty do you still perform when you know it will not change the outcome?

XIV.23.title: Not deceiving, but opposing
XIV.23.reflection: Zilu asks how to serve a ruler. Do not deceive him, and stand up to him. Loyalty includes open disagreement.
XIV.23.question: Whom do you serve that you should stand up to?

XIV.24.title: Up and down
XIV.24.reflection: The junzi goes upward; the small man goes downward. Legge reads it as progress. Others read it as understanding: the junzi understands what is high, the small man what is low.
XIV.24.question: In which direction did your attention go today?

XIV.25.title: Learning for oneself
XIV.25.reflection: In ancient times people learned for their own sake; now they learn for others' approval. Learning for oneself is not selfishness here: it means learning to become better, not to be seen.
XIV.25.question: What are you learning only so that others will see it?

XIV.26.title: A messenger indeed
XIV.26.reflection: Qu Boyu, an official of Wei, sends a messenger. What is your master doing? He wishes to reduce his faults and has not yet managed it. When the messenger leaves, the Master says twice: what a messenger! A modest answer that honours both master and servant.
XIV.26.question: How would someone who works with you describe what you are trying to do?

XIV.27.title: Not in the office, again
XIV.27.reflection: VIII.14 returns word for word. The compilers kept it twice, perhaps because it reached them twice, and the next chapter pairs it with Zengzi's version.
XIV.27.question: Since you first read it, has anything outside your responsibility occupied you?

XIV.28.title: Thoughts in their place
XIV.28.reflection: Master Zeng: the junzi does not let his thoughts go beyond his position. The thought is quoted from the Book of Changes, hexagram 52, Keeping Still. It is about attention as much as about rank: keep your mind on what is yours to do.
XIV.28.question: Where did your thoughts wander today beyond what was yours to do?

XIV.29.title: Words and deeds
XIV.29.reflection: The junzi is ashamed when his words exceed his deeds. Legge reads it as modest in speech and exceeding in action. The theme of the book, once more.
XIV.29.question: Where do your words exceed your deeds?

XIV.30.title: Three ways, none of them mine
XIV.30.reflection: The Way of the junzi has three parts, and I have none: the humane are not anxious, the wise not perplexed, the brave not afraid. Zigong says: Master, you are describing yourself. The teacher's modesty and the student's reply sit side by side.
XIV.30.question: Which of the three do others see in you that you do not?

XIV.31.title: Comparing people
XIV.31.reflection: Zigong liked to compare people. Ci must be very worthy; I have no time for that. A dry rebuke: judging others is a pastime of those who have finished with themselves.
XIV.31.question: Whom did you compare today, and what did it do for you?

XIV.32.title: My own lack of ability
XIV.32.reflection: Not troubled that others do not know me, troubled by my own inability. The worry of I.16 and IV.14 again, turned toward ability.
XIV.32.question: What ability would you most like to improve?

XIV.33.title: Not suspecting, and yet seeing
XIV.33.reflection: Not to anticipate deceit or suspect bad faith, and yet to be the first to notice it: is that not worthiness? Trust without naivety.
XIV.33.question: Are you more often too suspicious, or too slow to see?

XIV.34.title: Why so busy?
XIV.34.reflection: Weisheng Mu, a hermit, asks why Confucius keeps hurrying from place to place: is he trying to be a clever talker? I would not dare; I hate stubbornness. He means the stubbornness of those who give up on the world.
XIV.34.question: Is your persistence in something a virtue or obstinacy?

XIV.35.title: The virtue of a horse
XIV.35.reflection: A fine horse is praised not for its strength but for its character. Legge keeps the word ji for the famous horse. Character matters even in a horse.
XIV.35.question: What do you praise in others: their strength, or their character?

XIV.36.title: Repay injury with justice
XIV.36.reflection: Someone asks about repaying injury with kindness, a saying also found in the Tao Te Ching. Then with what will you repay kindness? Repay injury with uprightness, kindness with kindness. Confucius declines both revenge and unearned forgiveness, and asks for fairness.
XIV.36.question: Is there an injury you have repaid with more or less than justice?

XIV.37.title: Heaven knows me
XIV.37.reflection: No one knows me, says the Master. Zigong asks why. I do not complain against Heaven or blame people; I study things below and reach what is above. The one who knows me is Heaven. A lament without bitterness.
XIV.37.question: When you feel unknown, whom do you blame?

XIV.38.title: If the Way is to prevail
XIV.38.reflection: Gongbo Liao slanders Zilu to the Ji family, and an official offers to have him killed. If the Way prevails, it is fate; if it fails, it is fate; what can Gongbo Liao do against fate? Confucius refuses violence on his own behalf.
XIV.38.question: What would you refuse to do even to defend yourself?

XIV.39.title: Withdrawing
XIV.39.reflection: The worthy withdraw from the world; next, from a particular place; next, from a hostile look; next, from hostile words. Four degrees of retreat. The book takes the hermits seriously even when it argues with them.
XIV.39.question: From what have you withdrawn, and was it the right degree?

XIV.40.title: Seven men
XIV.40.reflection: Those who did so were seven. The chapter is a fragment; no one knows for sure which seven are meant. It shows the book as compiled from notes, some of which have lost their context.
XIV.40.question: What saying do you know whose context has been lost?

XIV.41.title: Knows it cannot be done
XIV.41.reflection: A gatekeeper at Shimen asks Zilu where he comes from. From Kong. Is that the one who knows it cannot be done, and still does it? An outsider's sentence that became one of the best descriptions of Confucius.
XIV.41.question: What do you keep doing though you know it may not succeed?

XIV.42.title: The man with the basket
XIV.42.reflection: Confucius plays the stone chimes in Wei, and a man with a basket passes and hears a stubborn heart: if no one knows you, stop; quoting an ode, deep water you wade through, shallow you lift your skirts. How determined he is, says the Master; that would not be hard. The hermit's withdrawal is easy; staying engaged is hard.
XIV.42.question: When is giving up the easy choice that looks wise?

XIV.43.title: Three years of silence
XIV.43.reflection: Zizhang asks about a king of old who did not speak for three years of mourning. Why only him? The ancients all did so: the ministers took orders from the chief minister for three years. Mourning as an institution, with the state carried on by others.
XIV.43.question: Who carries things for you when you cannot?

XIV.44.title: When those above love ritual
XIV.44.reflection: When those above love ritual, the people are easy to employ. The order of a state, once more, begins at the top.
XIV.44.question: Where are you above someone, and what do they learn from your example?

XIV.45.title: Cultivate yourself to bring peace
XIV.45.reflection: Zilu asks about the junzi: cultivate yourself with respect. Is that all? Cultivate yourself to bring peace to others. Is that all? Cultivate yourself to bring peace to all the people; even Yao and Shun found that hard. The answer widens three times, and each time it begins with the self.
XIV.45.question: Whom does your own self-cultivation bring peace to?

XIV.46.title: A tap on the shin
XIV.46.reflection: Yuan Rang, an old acquaintance, waits for the Master squatting rudely. Young and not respectful, grown and not accomplishing anything, old and not dying: a thief. And he taps him on the shin with his staff. The book keeps a moment of impatience, and perhaps of old familiarity.
XIV.46.question: With whom are you allowed to be impatient, because you go back a long way?

XIV.47.title: In a hurry to be grown
XIV.47.reflection: A boy from Que carries messages for the Master. Is he making progress? I see him take the seat of an adult and walk beside his elders. He is not seeking progress; he wants to be grown quickly. Hurry and progress are not the same.
XIV.47.question: What are you hurrying to be, instead of becoming?
